a3: You ask ChatGPT a question on a plane. Your message is about to travel further than your flight. A lot further. You're flying at 900 kilometres an hour. But your message doesn't go to the ground. It goes up. 36,000 kilometres up, to a satellite parked over the equator. Then all the way back down to a ground station, and into a data centre. The answer makes the same trip in reverse. That's about 143,000 kilometres. Three and a half times around the Earth. In about half a second. Unless your airline has Starlink. Then the satellite is only 550 kilometres up. So next time the wifi feels slow, remember where your message just went. What's the strangest thing you've asked AI on a flight?
a4: Ask an older AI how many R's are in strawberry, and it would say two. It could write you a poem in seconds. But it couldn't count three letters. Here's why. AI doesn't read letters. It reads tokens. Chunks of text, like str, aw and berry. To the model, strawberry is three puzzle pieces, not ten letters. So counting the R's is like counting the bricks inside a box you're not allowed to open. Newer models fixed it by thinking first, spelling the word out letter by letter. Which is exactly what you'd tell a kid to do. So how many R's are in strawberry? Be honest. Did you just count?
a5: Ask ChatGPT the exact same question twice, and you'll get two different answers. That's not a bug. It's on purpose. For every next word, the model has a list of options, each with a probability. The sky is blue, maybe ninety percent. Clear, six percent. Falling, one percent. If it always picked the top word, it would sound like a robot reading a manual. So it rolls weighted dice. Usually the favourite wins. Sometimes the underdog does. Developers even get a dial for it, called temperature. Turn it down, it plays safe. Turn it up, it gets creative. Turn it all the way up, and it stops making sense. So every answer you've ever had was one roll of the dice. Try it. Ask the same thing twice, and tell me which answer won.
a6: Last time, we found out the T in GPT came from Google. Now, the P. P stands for pre-trained. Sounds boring. It isn't. Before you ever typed a word, the model had already read a huge chunk of the internet. GPT-3 alone was trained on about 300 billion tokens. Reading that nonstop, day and night, would take you around 1,700 years. But here's the twist. It didn't memorise it. It learned patterns. How sentences usually go, and what usually comes next. That's the P. Everything it learned before it met you. And the G? That's next time. Which letter would you have guessed was the most important?
a7: In 2023, a lawyer in New York handed a judge six court cases. None of them existed. ChatGPT had made them up. The names, the dates, the quotes. All of it. He even asked it if they were real. It said yes. But it wasn't lying. Lying means you know the truth. AI doesn't look things up. It predicts what a good answer usually looks like. And a fake case can look exactly like a real one. That's called a hallucination. The lawyers were fined 5,000 dollars. So use it to draft. Never to check itself. Has AI ever told you something wrong, with total confidence?
a8: When ChatGPT says thinking, it's actually writing. You just can't see it. Reasoning models write a long, private draft before they answer you. They try an approach, check it, throw it away, and try again. Sometimes thousands of words, for a one line answer. And here's the part nobody tells you. Developers pay for every one of those hidden words. That's why hard questions take longer, and cost more. It's not thinking like you do. It's thinking out loud, with the volume off. So next time you see thinking, you'll know. Someone's writing an essay. What's the longest you've watched it think?
a9: Every time you send ChatGPT a message, it re-reads your entire chat. From the very first word. The model has no memory between messages. None. So the app quietly sends the whole conversation again, every single time. Message one, it reads one. Message fifty, it reads all fifty. That's why really long chats get slower. And at some point, it simply doesn't fit. Every model has a limit, called the context window. So the oldest parts get trimmed, and it starts forgetting how your chat began. That's why a fresh chat often gives better answers. How long is your longest chat right now?
